title: Extra information
theme: Non-defining relative clauses (extra information with commas)
goal: Student adds extra information to sentences using non-defining relative clauses with who, which, whose, where, when — distinguishing from defining clauses.
module_chunks: My brother, who lives in Rio,...
The Amazon, which is the longest river,...
Maria, whose father is a doctor,...
Paris, where I lived for a year,...
My friend, who I've known for years,...
The book, which won an award,...
Defining vs non-defining (no commas vs commas)

units.title: My brother, who
units.real_life_context: You add extra information about a specific person already identified.

grammar.sentence: My brother, _____ lives in Rio, is a teacher.
grammar.explanation: A non-defining relative clause for people uses "who" (never "that" in non-defining). Commas signal EXTRA information — not essential to identify the brother.

grammar.sentence: Maria, _____ I met yesterday, is from Spain.
grammar.explanation: "Who" for people in non-defining. "That" isn't used with commas. "Whom" would be formal, but "who" dominates current usage.

grammar.sentence: My boss, _____ is very strict, gave me a raise.
grammar.explanation: Non-defining: "who is very strict". "That" doesn't work in non-defining.

grammar.sentence: Tom, _____ I've known for years, just got married.
grammar.explanation: "Who I've known for years" — extra info about Tom. Specific person, commas.

grammar.sentence: My sister, _____ studies medicine, lives in São Paulo.
grammar.hint: relative pronoun para pessoa em non-defining
grammar.explanation: "Who studies medicine" — extra info about the sister. Specific.

grammar.sentence: Ana, _____ I work with, just had a baby.
grammar.explanation: "Who I work with" — extra info about Ana. Note: stranded preposition at the end is acceptable.

grammar.sentence: Mr. Silva, _____ teaches English, is from Portugal.
grammar.explanation: "Who teaches English" — extra information about a person already identified by name.

grammar.sentence: My brother, that lives in Rio, is a teacher.
grammar.answer: My brother, who lives in Rio, is a teacher.
grammar.explanation: Common error: using "that" in non-defining. "That" only in defining clauses (no commas). For non-defining: "who".

grammar.sentence: Maria who I met yesterday is from Spain.
grammar.answer: Maria, who I met yesterday, is from Spain.
grammar.explanation: Maria is already specific (proper name). The information is EXTRA, it doesn't identify. So, commas are needed (non-defining).

grammar.passage: My brother, who lives in Rio, is a teacher. Maria, who I met last week, is from Spain. My boss, who is very strict, gave me a raise. Mr. Silva, who teaches English, is from Portugal.
grammar.question: Who teaches English?
grammar.explanation: The text says "Mr. Silva, who teaches English, is from Portugal".

listening_speaking.text: My brother, who lives in Rio, is a teacher.
Maria, who I met yesterday, is great.
My boss, who is very strict, gave me a raise.
Tom, who I've known for years, just got married.
Ana, who I work with, just had a baby.

units.title: The Amazon, which
units.grammar_focus: Non-defining relative clauses with "which" (things) and clause-referring "which"
units.real_life_context: You add extra information about things, places, or even entire previous statements.

grammar.sentence: The Amazon, _____ is the longest river, runs through Brazil.
grammar.explanation: Non-defining for thing/place: "which". "That" doesn't work in non-defining. "The Amazon" is already identified, so the info is EXTRA.

grammar.sentence: My new phone, _____ I bought last week, broke already.
grammar.explanation: "Which I bought last week" — extra info about the specific phone. In non-defining, "which" is required.

grammar.sentence: She didn't call me back, _____ surprised me.
grammar.explanation: "Which" can refer to an entire previous CLAUSE. "Which surprised me" — the fact that she didn't call is what surprised me.

grammar.sentence: The book, _____ won an award, became a bestseller.
grammar.explanation: "Which won an award" — extra info about the book. Non-defining with "which".

grammar.sentence: Brazil, _____ is the largest country in South America, has many cultures.
grammar.explanation: "Which is the largest country" — extra information about Brazil.

grammar.sentence: My laptop, _____ I use every day, is getting old.
grammar.explanation: "Which I use every day" — extra info about the specific laptop.

grammar.sentence: He arrived two hours late, _____ made everyone angry.
grammar.explanation: "Which made everyone angry" — "which" refers to the fact that he arrived late. Clause-level referent.

grammar.sentence: The Amazon, that is the longest river, runs through Brazil.
grammar.answer: The Amazon, which is the longest river, runs through Brazil.
grammar.explanation: "That" only in defining clauses (no commas). For non-defining: "which".

grammar.sentence: My phone which I bought last week broke already.
grammar.answer: My phone, which I bought last week, broke already.
grammar.explanation: If the info is EXTRA (doesn't identify among several phones), use commas. Without commas, it would be defining (among several, the one I bought last week).

grammar.passage: The Amazon, which is the longest river in South America, runs through Brazil. My new phone, which I bought last week, broke already. The book, which won an award last year, became a bestseller. Brazil, which is the largest country in South America, has many cultures.
grammar.question: What happened to the new phone?
grammar.explanation: The text says "My new phone, which I bought last week, broke already".

listening_speaking.text: The Amazon, which is the longest river, runs through Brazil.
My phone, which I bought last week, broke.
He came late, which annoyed everyone.
The book, which won an award, became a bestseller.
Brazil, which has many cultures, is huge.

units.title: Maria, whose
units.real_life_context: You describe possessions or attributes of a person with extra information.

grammar.sentence: Maria, _____ father is a doctor, is studying medicine too.
grammar.explanation: "Whose" signals POSSESSION in a relative clause. "Maria, whose father..." — Maria's father. Works in both defining and non-defining.

grammar.sentence: My neighbor, _____ dog barks all night, is moving away.
grammar.explanation: "Whose dog" — the neighbor's dog. Possession. Don't confuse with "who's" (who is).

grammar.sentence: The author, _____ book I loved, is coming to town.
grammar.explanation: "Whose book" — the author's book. Possession.

grammar.sentence: Tom, _____ wife is from Spain, speaks fluent Spanish.
grammar.explanation: "Whose wife" — Tom's wife. Possession of a person.

grammar.sentence: My friend, _____ car is in the shop, took the bus today.
grammar.explanation: "Whose car" — the friend's car.

grammar.sentence: The singer, _____ songs are famous worldwide, is from Brazil.
grammar.explanation: "Whose songs" — the singer's songs.

grammar.sentence: Mrs. Garcia, _____ children study with mine, is a great teacher.
grammar.explanation: "Whose children" — Mrs. Garcia's children.

grammar.sentence: Maria, who's father is a doctor, is studying medicine.
grammar.answer: Maria, whose father is a doctor, is studying medicine.
grammar.explanation: "Who's" = "who is" (contraction). "Whose" = possession. Common error: confusing them because of identical pronunciation.

grammar.sentence: My neighbor, that dog barks all night, is moving.
grammar.answer: My neighbor, whose dog barks all night, is moving.
grammar.explanation: "That" doesn't work for possession or in non-defining. To show whose dog it is: "whose".

grammar.passage: Maria, whose father is a doctor, is studying medicine. My neighbor, whose dog barks all night, is moving. The author, whose book I loved, is coming to town. Tom, whose wife is from Spain, speaks fluent Spanish.
grammar.question: Why does Tom speak fluent Spanish?
grammar.explanation: The text says "Tom, whose wife is from Spain, speaks fluent Spanish".

listening_speaking.text: Maria, whose father is a doctor, is studying medicine.
My neighbor, whose dog barks, is moving.
The author, whose book I loved, is here.
Tom, whose wife is from Spain, speaks Spanish.
The singer, whose songs are famous, is Brazilian.

units.title: Where, when
units.real_life_context: You add extra information about places and time periods.

grammar.sentence: Paris, _____ I lived for a year, is beautiful.
grammar.explanation: "Where" for place in non-defining. "Paris, where I lived" = "in Paris". More natural than "which".

grammar.sentence: 2020, _____ the pandemic started, was a hard year.
grammar.explanation: "When" for time in non-defining. "In 2020, the pandemic started" → "2020, when the pandemic started".

grammar.sentence: My hometown, _____ I grew up, is small.
grammar.explanation: "Where I grew up" — the place I'm from. Non-defining "where".

grammar.sentence: The summer of 2018, _____ I traveled to Europe, was unforgettable.
grammar.explanation: "When I traveled" — specific time in non-defining.

grammar.sentence: São Paulo, _____ I work, is a huge city.
grammar.explanation: "Where I work" — specific place of work.

grammar.sentence: March, _____ I was born, is my favorite month.
grammar.explanation: "When I was born" — specific time.

grammar.sentence: The university, _____ I studied, is famous.
grammar.explanation: "Where I studied" — place of study.

grammar.sentence: Paris, which I lived for a year, is beautiful.
grammar.hint: Para LUGAR de habitação, "where" é mais natural
grammar.answer: Paris, where I lived for a year, is beautiful.
grammar.explanation: "Which" would work in a structure like "which I visited" (direct object), but for "in Paris" (place of residence), "where" is correct.

grammar.sentence: 2020, which the pandemic started, was hard.
grammar.answer: 2020, when the pandemic started, was hard.
grammar.explanation: Years, months, moments → "when". "Which" doesn't work for time.

grammar.passage: Paris, where I lived for a year, is beautiful. 2020, when the pandemic started, was a hard year. My hometown, where I grew up, is small. The summer of 2018, when I traveled to Europe, was unforgettable.
grammar.question: Where did the speaker grow up?
grammar.explanation: The text says "My hometown, where I grew up, is small".

listening_speaking.text: Paris, where I lived for a year, is beautiful.
2020, when the pandemic started, was hard.
My hometown, where I grew up, is small.
The summer of 2018, when I traveled, was unforgettable.

units.title: Defining vs non-defining
units.grammar_focus: Difference between defining (no commas, "that" OK) and non-defining (commas, no "that")
units.real_life_context: You distinguish essential identifying info from extra info.

grammar.sentence: Defining: "The man _____ called me is my boss." (which type?)
grammar.explanation: "Who" works in both — defining and non-defining for people. "That" also works in defining. Since there are no commas, it's defining.

grammar.sentence: Non-defining: "My boss, _____ called me, gave me a raise."
grammar.explanation: Commas = non-defining. "That" does NOT work in non-defining. Only "who".

grammar.sentence: Defining: "The book _____ I bought yesterday is great."
grammar.explanation: Defining (no commas) with object: "that" or "which" or nothing. "That" is the most natural in defining.

grammar.sentence: Non-defining: "This book, _____ I bought yesterday, is great."
grammar.explanation: Commas = non-defining. "Which" required (not "that").

grammar.sentence: Defining: "The woman _____ lives next door is a doctor."
grammar.explanation: Defining identifies WHO (among several women). "Who" works; "that" does too.

grammar.sentence: Non-defining: "My mother, _____ is a doctor, lives next door."
grammar.explanation: "My mother" is already specific (only one). The info is EXTRA, not identifying.

grammar.sentence: Defining: "The town _____ I grew up is small."
grammar.explanation: Defining "where" with no commas. "The town where I grew up" — identifies which town.

grammar.sentence: Non-defining: "My brother, that lives in Rio, is a teacher."
grammar.answer: My brother, who lives in Rio, is a teacher.
grammar.explanation: Most common error: "that" in non-defining. Only defining allows "that". Non-defining: "who" or "which".

grammar.sentence: Defining mas sem vírgulas: "The man who called me yesterday is my boss." Está correto?
grammar.answer: The man who called me yesterday is my boss.
grammar.explanation: The sentence is already correct. "The man who called" — identifies WHICH man (among several). Defining, no commas.

grammar.passage: The man who called me yesterday is my boss (defining — identifies which man). My boss, who called me yesterday, is great (non-defining — extra info about the only boss). The book that I bought is fascinating (defining). This book, which won an award, is fascinating (non-defining).
grammar.question: When do you use commas?
grammar.explanation: The text explains that commas appear in non-defining clauses (extra information).

listening_speaking.text: The man who called is my boss.
My boss, who called me, is great.
The book that won the prize is on the table.
This book, which won the prize, is fascinating.
The town where I was born is small.

cross_unit_consolidation: Distinção entre defining (essencial, sem vírgulas) e non-defining (extra, com vírgulas)
"Which" pode se referir a uma cláusula inteira
